lessons.name: Collaborative operation modes (cobots)
lessons.summary: Collaborative operation modes describe how a robot application manages people sharing its workspace, rather than declaring an arm universally safe.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Collaborative operation modes describe how a robot application manages people sharing its workspace, rather than declaring an arm universally safe.

![Collaborative robot arm working near an operator](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-modes.webp)
*A cobot application pictured in Universal Robots’ explanation of collaborative operation. Source: [Publisher](https://www.universal-robots.com/blog/demystifying-cobot-safety-the-four-types-of-collaborative-operation/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** an arm sorting parts beside a student needs a plan for entry, teaching, normal motion, and unexpected contact.
- **Application, not label:** the gripper, carried object, surroundings, and task can introduce hazards even when the arm is marketed as a cobot.

## How it works
- **Software analogy:** choose an access-control policy for each application state, rather than trusting a server because its framework supports authentication.
- **Safety-rated monitored stop:** hazardous robot motion stops while a person occupies the shared area; the stop is monitored by the safety system.
- **Hand guiding:** a person directly guides robot movement using the intended enabling arrangement.
- **Speed and separation monitoring:** the system changes robot motion to maintain a protective distance from people.
- **Power and force limiting:** the application limits contact effects where contact is permitted by its risk assessment.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Task and hazards] --> B[Choose protective approach]
  B --> C[Configure application]
  C --> D[Validate protection]
  D --> E[Operate and monitor]
```

- **Worked example:** for a simulated sorting cell, use a monitored-stop state during part loading; do not assume that the same rule covers guided teaching.

> **Key idea:** Collaboration is a property of the whole task and its protection, not a permission sticker on a robot.

## Key terms
- **Cobot**: A robot intended for collaborative applications, not a guarantee that every installed task is safe.
- **Collaborative operation**: People and robots sharing an application workspace under defined protective conditions.
- **Safety-rated**: Designed and validated to meet specified safety-performance requirements.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Start with Robot safety standards & risk assessment to identify hazards before choosing a mode.
- **After:** Compare Speed & separation monitoring implementation with Collision detection & reaction (power and force limiting).

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Sketch a cell:** draw an arm, gripper, loading area, and operator in a notebook.
2. **List activities:** separate loading, automatic sorting, and guided teaching; give each a different state.
3. **Implement a mock state machine:** log allowed transitions when a simulated person enters or leaves.
4. **Explain one gap:** add a sharp carried object and identify why the arm’s collaborative label does not resolve it.

lessons.name: Collision detection & reaction (power and force limiting)
lessons.summary: Power and force limiting manages the consequences of robot contact by combining application design, contact sensing, motion limits, and an appropriate reaction.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Power and force limiting manages the consequences of robot contact by combining application design, contact sensing, motion limits, and an appropriate reaction.

![Published diagram from collision detection through classification to robot reaction](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-collision.webp)
*Figure 1 of the adaptive collision-sensitivity paper; extracted from the published PDF. Source: [Publisher](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.20184), Creative Commons Attribution License.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** a sorting arm’s elbow can contact someone even when its gripper follows a collision-free path.
- **Contact matters:** a brief bump and trapping a hand against a table are different hazards; detecting a bump does not undo its initial impact.

## How it works
- **Sense contact:** joint torque sensing or tactile skin can indicate an external interaction with the robot.
- **Localize and interpret:** determine which link touched something, estimate relevant contact effects, and select the configured reaction.
- **Research example:** Adaptive Collision Sensitivity uses contact location and estimated collision force to decide whether motion should stop, instead of one fixed threshold everywhere.
- **Software analogy:** an exception handler reacts after an event; resource limits and input restrictions must also reduce what can go wrong beforehand.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Contact sensing] --> B[Locate contact]
  B --> C[Estimate effects]
  C --> D[Select reaction]
  D --> E[Robot response]
```

- **Worked example:** replay a synthetic elbow-contact event and a gripper-contact event. Log location and reaction separately, rather than treating every event as an identical Boolean.

> **Key idea:** A contact detector is one component of protection, not proof that every collision is acceptable.

> **Watch out:** Do not tune collision thresholds by deliberately striking or trapping a person.

## Key terms
- **Torque**: Turning effort around a joint.
- **Tactile skin**: A distributed contact-sensitive surface on the robot.
- **Constrained contact**: Contact where a body part can become trapped rather than moving freely away.
- **PFL**: Power and force limiting: protection that restricts the effects of permitted physical contact.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Read Collaborative operation modes (cobots) and Impedance & admittance control for the application and contact-control context.
- **After:** Connect contact protection to Safe learning & safety filters and Robot safety standards & risk assessment.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Watch the research demo:** identify detection, localization, and reaction as separate stages.
2. **Create synthetic events:** label contact location and whether the imagined contact is constrained.
3. **Write a simulator-only handler:** map events to logged reactions without connecting hardware.
4. **Review omissions:** list the tool shape, payload, and trapping geometry your toy handler cannot assess.

lessons.name: Conversational & multimodal robot interfaces
lessons.summary: A conversational, multimodal robot interface combines channels such as speech, vision, and expressive motion so people can communicate with a robot.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
A conversational, multimodal robot interface combines channels such as speech, vision, and expressive motion so people can communicate with a robot.

![Reachy Mini expressive tabletop robot shown by its creators](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-interfaces.webp)
*Reachy Mini in its creators’ introduction to conversational, expressive robotics. Source: [Publisher](https://huggingface.co/blog/reachy-mini), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** a tabletop robot hears “look here,” turns toward the speaker, and acknowledges that it understood.
- **Visible feedback:** listening, thinking, speaking, and failing should look different; otherwise a person cannot tell whether to repeat a request.

## How it works
- **Speech input:** capture microphone audio and convert it into words, or use a model that handles audio directly.
- **Additional context:** camera observations and the conversation history can help interpret a request, but can also introduce ambiguity.
- **Response output:** coordinate spoken replies with gaze or expressive movement rather than launching unrelated actions.
- **Software analogy:** this is an event-driven service with several input streams; timestamps, cancellation, and explicit state prevent stale events from triggering fresh actions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Audio and visual events] --> B[Interpret context]
  B --> C[Choose response]
  C --> D[Speech and expression]
  D --> E[Observe user response]
  E --> B
```

- **Worked example:** in a text-only mockup, “stop talking” cancels queued speech immediately; “look at that” produces a clarification request when no referent is available.
- **Concrete reference:** Reachy Mini’s conversation app is a published example connecting dialogue with an expressive robot interface.

> **Key idea:** A useful interface coordinates communication and repair, not just language-model replies.

## Key terms
- **Modality**: A communication channel, such as speech, images, or movement.
- **Turn-taking**: Coordinating when each participant speaks or acts.
- **Speech recognition**: Converting recorded speech into text.
- **Grounding**: Connecting a word or instruction to the relevant object, event, or shared context.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Use HRI foundations & user-study methods to choose a communication task and an observable success criterion.
- **After:** Combine Human detection & body-pose tracking for HRI with Semantic safety & guardrails for LLM/VLA-controlled robots.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Watch the Reachy Mini demo:** note how expression accompanies conversation.
2. **Build a terminal mockup:** represent listening, responding, and cancelled states with printed messages.
3. **Replay interruptions:** inject a cancellation event while a reply is queued, then verify it never plays.
4. **Try ambiguous requests:** record whether clarification prevents a wrong response; keep cameras and physical motion disabled.

lessons.name: HRI foundations & user-study methods
lessons.summary: Human–robot interaction studies how people and robots affect each other, using explicit tasks and evidence rather than a convincing demonstration alone.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Human–robot interaction studies how people and robots affect each other, using explicit tasks and evidence rather than a convincing demonstration alone.

![Published illustration of a quadruped robot and a participant route in a study space](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-studies.webp)
*The Safe Spot paper illustrates a study setup for evaluating perceived safety around a quadruped. Source: [Publisher](https://arxiv.org/html/2403.05400), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** a robot that finishes sorting quickly may still confuse the person waiting to load it.
- **Different questions:** “Did the task succeed?” and “Did the person feel safe?” need different measurements; neither substitutes for physical safety validation.

## How it works
- **Start with a question:** does an acknowledgement cue help people recognize that a robot received their request?
- **Compare conditions:** use the same task with the cue enabled and disabled; change one design feature rather than the whole interface.
- **Measure behavior:** record completed tasks, misunderstandings, and completion times alongside participants’ comments.
- **Measure experience:** questionnaires such as Godspeed collect ratings of qualities including perceived safety and likeability.
- **Software analogy:** treat a study like an A/B test with a written protocol; changing the task halfway through makes the result hard to interpret.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Research question] --> B[Task and conditions]
  B --> C[Consented sessions]
  C --> D[Behavior and ratings]
  D --> E[Analyze limitations]
```

- **Worked example:** compare two recorded robot-interface clips, one with acknowledgement and one without. Ask the same question after each and alternate presentation order across volunteers.

> **Key idea:** Decide what evidence would answer your question before showing anyone the robot.

## Key terms
- **Condition**: One version of the system or situation being compared.
- **Dependent measure**: The outcome recorded, such as errors or a questionnaire rating.
- **Confound**: An unintended difference that could explain an observed result.
- **Perceived safety**: How safe an interaction feels to a participant, distinct from measured physical risk.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Begin with a small, observable interaction; no robot hardware is required for a first study.
- **After:** Apply the method to Legible & expressive robot motion and Social & human-aware navigation.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Write one hypothesis:** predict a specific observable difference between two interface clips.
2. **Prepare a protocol:** use identical instructions and explain voluntary participation and data handling.
3. **Run a tiny pilot:** collect task responses and one clearly labelled experience rating.
4. **Report honestly:** show individual observations and confounds; a small convenience sample does not establish a universal result.

lessons.name: Human detection & body-pose tracking for HRI
lessons.summary: Human detection finds people in sensor data; body-pose tracking follows estimated body landmarks over time so a robot can reason about nearby movement.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Human detection finds people in sensor data; body-pose tracking follows estimated body landmarks over time so a robot can reason about nearby movement.

![MediaPipe diagram labeling human body landmarks](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-pose.webp)
*MediaPipe’s published landmark map labels the body points returned by its pose model. Source: [Publisher](https://ai.google.dev/edge/mediapipe/solutions/vision/pose_landmarker), Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 License.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** a screen-based assistant can acknowledge a raised hand without needing to identify who owns it.
- **Different outputs:** a person detector gives a region containing someone; a pose model estimates structured landmarks such as shoulders, elbows, and wrists.

## How it works
- **Process frames:** MediaPipe Pose Landmarker accepts images, video, or a live stream and estimates body landmarks.
- **Read coordinates carefully:** normalized image coordinates describe positions within the image; world-coordinate output uses a different coordinate convention.
- **Preserve time:** attach frame timestamps so downstream code can reject stale observations instead of reacting to an old hand position.
- **Software analogy:** a pose result is a typed API response, not ground truth; validate its fields and uncertainty before using it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Camera frame] --> B[Find person]
  B --> C[Estimate landmarks]
  C --> D[Check confidence and time]
  D --> E[Gesture state]
```

- **Worked example:** compare a wrist’s vertical image coordinate with its shoulder’s coordinate to suggest “hand raised.” Treat missing or low-quality landmarks as unknown, not as a lowered hand.
- **Privacy choice:** a gesture demo can display landmarks without saving identifiable footage.

> **Key idea:** A missing or uncertain landmark is unknown data, not evidence that a person is absent.

> **Watch out:** A webcam pose model is not a safety-rated presence sensor for protecting people from robot motion.

## Key terms
- **Landmark**: An estimated anatomical point, such as an elbow or wrist.
- **Occlusion**: A body part being hidden from the camera.
- **Tracking**: Connecting observations across successive frames.
- **Normalized coordinate**: An image-relative coordinate rather than a physical distance in the room.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Human body & hand pose tracking provides the perception context; basic Python image processing is enough for a screen-only start.
- **After:** Feed timestamped observations into Human motion & intention prediction or Conversational & multimodal robot interfaces.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Open the Python guide:** choose recorded video or a webcam with the participant’s consent.
2. **Render landmarks:** draw the returned skeleton on screen; do not command robot motion.
3. **Implement a gesture state:** distinguish raised, lowered, and unknown using wrist and shoulder observations.
4. **Test missing data:** cover an arm and leave the frame; log when confidence or freshness fails.

lessons.name: Human motion & intention prediction
lessons.summary: Human motion prediction estimates plausible future movement, while intention prediction reasons about likely goals without assuming a person’s plan is certain.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Human motion prediction estimates plausible future movement, while intention prediction reasons about likely goals without assuming a person’s plan is certain.

![Published Trajectron++ road-scene diagram with pedestrians and alternative future directions](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-prediction.webp)
*Trajectron++ illustrates interacting agents and several possible future movement directions. Source: [Publisher](https://arxiv.org/html/2001.03093v5), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** a delivery robot approaching a crossing needs more than a pedestrian’s current position; either participant may turn or stop.
- **Planning benefit:** several plausible futures let a planner avoid committing to the single path that would fail if the person changes direction.

## How it works
- **Build a history:** track positions over time, keeping timestamps and a consistent coordinate frame.
- **Condition on context:** neighboring agents, scene structure, and motion constraints can change which futures are plausible.
- **Forecast alternatives:** Trajectron++ models multiple interacting agents and produces dynamically feasible trajectory forecasts, rather than only a straight-line extrapolation.
- **Software analogy:** this resembles speculative execution with several branches; the planner must remain correct when its favorite branch is wrong.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Track history] --> B[Agents and scene context]
  B --> C[Possible future paths]
  C --> D[Conservative plan]
  D --> E[New observation]
  E --> A
```

- **Worked example:** draw a pedestrian approaching a junction, then keep both left-turn and straight-ahead futures. A toy planner waits if either future crosses its intended path.
- **Evaluate honestly:** compare forecasts against held-out observed motion; a plausible-looking line alone does not establish useful prediction.

> **Key idea:** Prediction should widen your view of possible futures, not turn a guess into permission to approach someone.

## Key terms
- **Trajectory**: A sequence of positions over time.
- **Multimodal prediction**: A forecast containing distinct plausible futures, not merely several sensor types.
- **Intention**: A hypothesized goal underlying someone’s actions.
- **Dynamically feasible**: Consistent with the modeled agent’s motion constraints.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Use Human detection & body-pose tracking for HRI and Kalman filtering & multisensor fusion to understand noisy time-series inputs.
- **After:** Apply forecasts to Social & human-aware navigation and Speed & separation monitoring implementation, without replacing protective sensing.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Create a toy track:** record a moving dot approaching a junction in a small Python animation.
2. **Implement a baseline:** extrapolate recent velocity and plot its forecast.
3. **Add alternatives:** include stopping and turning; mark your choices as hand-written hypotheses, not learned probabilities.
4. **Replay a surprise:** turn the dot unexpectedly and compare a single-path planner with an alternative-aware planner.

lessons.name: Human-robot handovers
lessons.summary: A human–robot handover transfers an object between a person and a robot through coordinated approach, grasping, and release.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
A human–robot handover transfers an object between a person and a robot through coordinated approach, grasping, and release.

![Simulated receiving arm approaching an offered object in HandoverSim](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-handovers.webp)
*A frame from the HandoverSim authors’ published demonstration. Source: [Publisher](https://github.com/NVlabs/handover-sim), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** receiving a mug is not just grasping it; the robot must avoid the giver’s hand and establish support before the giver releases.
- **Two coupled agents:** object pose, human grasp, timing, and communication all matter; a fixed pick-and-place script misses the exchange itself.

## How it works
- **Pre-handover phase:** identify the offered object and approach a useful receiving pose without interfering with the person’s grasp.
- **Physical exchange:** establish the receiving grasp, coordinate load transfer, and release only when the exchange conditions are satisfied.
- **Research reference:** HandoverSim separates pre-handover motion and physical exchange to evaluate human-to-robot object handovers in simulation.
- **Software analogy:** think of a two-party commit: approaching is preparation, but ownership should not switch until both sides have reached the required state.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Offer object] --> B[Plan approach]
  B --> C[Establish grasp]
  C --> D[Confirm transfer]
  D --> E[Release and retreat]
```

- **Worked example:** in a mock mug handover, the receiving agent reports “ready” only after its grasp state is valid. Removing the readiness signal keeps the giver’s release transition disabled.
- **Evaluation:** inspect failed approaches separately from failed exchanges so a successful reach cannot hide an unreliable transfer.

> **Key idea:** A handover succeeds when support transfers reliably, not when a gripper merely reaches the object.

> **Watch out:** Keep your first exchange simulated; premature release can drop an object onto someone.

## Key terms
- **Handover**: A coordinated transfer of an object between agents.
- **Receiving pose**: The position and orientation chosen for the receiver’s grasp.
- **Load transfer**: The change in which agent supports the object’s weight.
- **Pre-handover**: The preparation and approach before the physical exchange.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Start with HRI foundations & user-study methods and Legible & expressive robot motion to reason about coordination cues.
- **After:** Combine Human motion & intention prediction with Collision detection & reaction (power and force limiting).

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Watch the HandoverSim video:** identify where approach ends and physical exchange begins.
2. **Implement two agents:** represent giver and receiver as state machines with a shared virtual object.
3. **Add a readiness handshake:** transfer ownership only after the receiving grasp becomes valid.
4. **Inject failures:** delay readiness or withdraw the offer; verify that your simulation never releases an unsupported object.

lessons.name: Learning from human feedback & corrections
lessons.summary: Learning from human feedback updates a robot policy using evaluations or corrections gathered while the robot attempts a task.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Learning from human feedback updates a robot policy using evaluations or corrections gathered while the robot attempts a task.

![I3L figure illustrating a human correction during robot execution](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-feedback.webp)
*The I3L project’s published correction example. Source: [Publisher](https://i-3l.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** a simulated arm repeatedly reaches beside a cup; a person takes over at that mistake and demonstrates a recovery.
- **Data value:** corrections target states the current policy actually visits, including awkward states missing from a clean demonstration dataset.

## How it works
- **Run a policy:** the learned controller proposes an action from its current observation.
- **Allow intervention:** a human may correct behavior or temporarily take control; log what the policy saw and what the person actually did.
- **Collect then retrain:** add appropriate labelled examples and evaluate the updated policy on separate attempts.
- **Research reference:** HG-DAgger uses human interventions; I3L studies iterative corrections for whole-body mobile manipulation.
- **Software analogy:** corrections resemble useful bug reproductions plus patches; committing a patch does not prove that previously working tests still pass.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Policy attempt] --> B[Human correction]
  B --> C[Label and store data]
  C --> D[Retrain policy]
  D --> E[Held-out evaluation]
  E --> A
```

- **Worked example:** when a virtual cursor misses its target, record the observation and a corrected direction. Keep uncorrected policy actions distinguishable from human-labelled actions.
- **Separate feedback types:** a scalar rating says how good an attempt was; an action correction specifies what to do instead. Training code must not silently interchange them.

> **Key idea:** A correction is training evidence; only separate evaluation tells you whether the new policy improved.

## Key terms
- **Policy**: A function mapping observations to proposed actions.
- **Intervention**: A person interrupting or replacing the policy’s control.
- **Distribution shift**: A mismatch between training situations and situations encountered during execution.
- **Held-out evaluation**: Testing on attempts not used to train the updated model.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Read Imitation learning (behavior cloning) and Interactive imitation & human-in-the-loop correction before implementing a training loop.
- **After:** Connect Shared control & shared autonomy with Safe learning & safety filters when collecting corrections.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Watch I3L’s correction examples:** distinguish operator takeover from autonomous execution.
2. **Build a cursor task:** use a simple policy to move a dot toward a target.
3. **Record interventions:** save observations, human actions, timestamps, and an explicit control-owner label.
4. **Retrain and compare:** test on unseen target positions; report both success and how often the human still intervenes.

lessons.name: Legible & expressive robot motion
lessons.summary: Legible motion makes a robot’s intended goal easier to infer, while expressive motion communicates additional interaction cues through movement.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Legible motion makes a robot’s intended goal easier to infer, while expressive motion communicates additional interaction cues through movement.

![HERB robot reaching toward objects along different trajectories](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-legibility.webp)
*A published comparison of robot reaching motions in the Robohub legibility article. Source: [Publisher](https://robohub.org/planning-robot-motions-that-humans-can-relate-to/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** an arm reaching between two cups can reveal its chosen cup early, reducing uncertainty for the person sharing the table.
- **More than smoothness:** a smooth trajectory can still hide its destination; a short path is not automatically an understandable path.

## How it works
- **Predictability asks:** given the goal, does this motion match what an observer expects?
- **Legibility asks:** given the partial motion, which goal does an observer infer?
- **Plan for the observer:** a trajectory may initially separate from another goal’s direction to communicate the intended destination.
- **Software analogy:** predictable motion resembles code following familiar conventions; legible motion resembles an informative progress indicator that reveals which operation is underway.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Candidate goals] --> B[Choose communicative path]
  B --> C[Show partial motion]
  C --> D[Human infers goal]
  D --> E[Evaluate interpretation]
```

- **Research nuance:** Generating Legible Motion constrains optimization so a supposedly helpful deviation does not become confusingly surprising.
- **Worked example:** animate a dot choosing the left of two targets. Compare a direct path with a path that separates toward the left earlier; pause both before arrival.
- **Measure the message:** ask viewers which target they expect, not merely which animation they prefer.

> **Key idea:** A motion can be easy to expect without making its destination easy to guess.

## Key terms
- **Legibility**: How well observed motion reveals its intended goal.
- **Predictability**: How expected a motion is when its goal is already known.
- **Trajectory**: The robot’s path through positions over time.
- **Expressive motion**: Movement designed to communicate an interaction cue beyond reaching a position.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Use HRI foundations & user-study methods to turn “looks clearer” into a measurable question.
- **After:** Apply these ideas to Human-robot handovers and Conversational & multimodal robot interfaces.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Watch the Berkeley demonstrations:** note how motion communicates intent to an observer.
2. **Animate two paths:** keep start, goal, and playback duration identical in a browser canvas.
3. **Pause before arrival:** ask consenting classmates to guess the destination, alternating clip order.
4. **Compare guesses:** record accuracy and uncertainty; explain why a clearer goal signal still says nothing about collision protection.

lessons.summary: Hand-guiding lets a person physically direct robot movement; kinesthetic teaching records that guidance as examples or waypoints for later robot behavior.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Hand-guiding lets a person physically direct robot movement; kinesthetic teaching records that guidance as examples or waypoints for later robot behavior.

![Helping Hand interface for controlling kinesthetic robot guidance](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-guiding.webp)
*ReconCycle’s Helping Hand interface exposes controls used during kinesthetic guidance. Source: [Publisher](https://reconcycle.github.io/standalone/kinesthetic/index.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Lab example:** a person guides an arm through a convenient approach to a workpiece instead of typing every joint position.
- **Separate purposes:** moving an arm into a useful pose and collecting a reusable training demonstration may share an interface, but need different recording logic.

## How it works
- **Enable guidance:** the intended robot mode and controls must allow deliberate physical guidance rather than fighting the normal position controller.
- **Respond to contact:** compliant control lets the robot yield in a defined way; gravity compensation can reduce the effort needed to support the arm.
- **Record meaningfully:** capture the robot state and timestamps, plus relevant events such as gripper opening, instead of saving an unexplained position list.
- **Software analogy:** this resembles recording a macro; replaying cursor coordinates is fragile unless the application context and event ordering also match.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Enable guidance] --> B[Person guides arm]
  B --> C[Record states and events]
  C --> D[Review demonstration]
  D --> E[Simulated replay]
```

- **Worked example:** for a virtual transfer, save approach, grasp, lift, and release events with their poses. During replay, check that “grasp” precedes “lift.”
- **Reference interface:** ReconCycle documents a Helping Hand interface for kinesthetic guidance, while Franka’s materials show guided robot interaction.

> **Key idea:** A useful demonstration records task events and context, not only the route the arm followed.

> **Watch out:** Never push a powered arm into compliance; only its intended guidance mode can provide the expected response.

## Key terms
- **Kinesthetic teaching**: Teaching by physically moving the robot through a demonstration.
- **Compliance**: A controlled willingness to move under applied force.
- **Gravity compensation**: Controller effort that counteracts the robot’s modeled weight.
- **Waypoint**: A recorded intermediate robot configuration or end-effector pose.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Read Impedance & admittance control and Collaborative operation modes (cobots) to distinguish yielding control from application protection.
- **After:** Use demonstrations in Imitation learning (behavior cloning) and Learning from human feedback & corrections.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Inspect the guidance interface:** identify enable controls, guidance settings, and the difference between movement and recording.
2. **Mock a recording:** create timestamped virtual poses and explicit gripper events in Python.
3. **Validate event order:** reject a recording that lifts before grasping or has non-increasing timestamps.
4. **Replay on screen:** draw the recorded path and events; compare a smooth-looking path with a semantically correct sequence.

lessons.name: Robot safety standards & risk assessment
lessons.summary: Robot safety risk assessment means listing every way a robot could hurt someone, rating each risk, and adding measures until what remains is acceptable.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Robot safety risk assessment means listing every way a robot could hurt someone, rating each risk, and adding measures until what remains is acceptable.

![Collaborative robot arm working in front of racks of 3D printers](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-assessment.webp)
*A cobot working inside a printer cell, the kind of setup a risk assessment describes. Source: [Robotiq blog](https://blog.robotiq.com/how-to-perform-a-risk-assessment-for-collaborative-robots), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Required before production:** Robotiq's guide states a risk assessment must be done for any collaborative robot before it goes into production.
- **Shared vocabulary:** standards give names to hazards, risks and safeguards, so a lab, a sponsor and an integrator mean the same thing.

## How it works
Think of it as a **threat model** for a web service, but the attacker is physics. You list what can go wrong, rate it, then patch the worst items first.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Describe the robot cell] --> B[Identify hazards]
  B --> C[Estimate risk]
  C --> D[Evaluate: acceptable?]
  D -- no --> E[Add risk reduction]
  E --> C
  D -- yes --> F[Document and verify]
```

- **ISO 12100:2010:** the general machinery method, with procedures for identifying hazards and estimating, evaluating and reducing risk across the machine life cycle.
- **ISO 10218-1:2025:** safety requirements for the industrial robot itself, treated as partly completed machinery.
- **ISO 10218-2:2025:** safety of the full robot application and cell, from integration to decommissioning.
- **ISO 13482:2014:** personal care robots (mobile servant, physical assistant, person carrier); not for robots faster than 20 km/h.
- **ISO/TS 15066:2016:** extra requirements for collaborative industrial robots, supplementing ISO 10218.
- **Four rating variables:** Robotiq's eBook rates each hazard by possible harm, likelihood of the event, possibility of avoidance and frequency of exposure.

> **Key idea:** Safety is a documented loop: you keep adding measures and re-rating until every listed hazard is acceptable.

> **Watch out:** ISO 12100 and ISO 13482 are both marked "to be revised" on iso.org, so check the current edition before citing one.

## Key terms
- **Hazard**: A potential source of harm, such as a moving link or a pinch point.
- **Risk**: The combination of how severe the harm is and how likely it is to happen.
- **Risk reduction**: Measures that lower risk, such as design changes, guards or speed limits.
- **Partly completed machinery**: A machine, like a bare robot arm, that is safe only once integrated into a cell.

## Before / after
- **Before:** No prerequisites; a basic picture of how a robot arm moves helps.
- **After:** Robotics regulation & compliance in the EU, Collaborative operation modes (cobots), Speed & separation monitoring implementation, and Safety of humanoids & dynamically stable mobile robots.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Describe your cell:** write the robot, gripper, task and who can approach it, for one lab demo arm.
2. **List hazards:** walk through each motion and note crushing, pinching, impact and electrical risks.
3. **Rate each row:** score harm, likelihood, avoidance and exposure in a spreadsheet, as in Robotiq's eBook.
4. **Add measures:** propose a reduction for the three worst rows and rate them again.
5. **Write limits:** state what your assessment does not cover, a section Robotiq's guide also recommends.

lessons.name: Robotics regulation & compliance in the EU
lessons.summary: To sell or deploy a robot in the EU you must follow laws, mainly the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 and the AI Act, not only voluntary standards.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
To sell or deploy a robot in the EU you must follow laws, mainly the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 and the AI Act, not only voluntary standards.

![Orange SIASUN industrial robot arm in a factory](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-eu.webp)
*A SIASUN industrial robot; new SIASUN models received CE certification under the EU Machinery Directive in 2024. Source: [SIASUN](https://en.siasun.com/new-model-industrial-robots-certified-with-eu-ce-marking.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **CE marking:** SIASUN calls the CE mark mandatory in the EU market and a "passport" for entering it.
- **New dates:** the Machinery Regulation applies on a mandatory basis from 20 January 2027, so lab demos built now meet the new rules.

## How it works
A **standard** is like a style guide; a **law** is like a compiler error. Laws set mandatory essential requirements, and harmonised standards are the usual way to show you meet them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Robot product] --> B[Which laws apply?]
  B --> C[Machinery Regulation]
  B --> D[AI Act]
  C --> E[Risk assessment and standards]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Declaration of conformity]
  F --> G[CE marking]
```

- **Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC:** the current law; machinery placed on the market before 20 January 2027 must comply with it.
- **Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230:** adopted 14 June 2023; it adds provisions for AI-powered safety functions and cyber-safety of safety control software.
- **Higher-risk machinery:** the Regulation addresses conformity assessment for machinery presenting a higher risk factor.
- **AI Act (EU) 2024/1689:** a risk-based law with four risk levels, from banned practices down to minimal risk.
- **High-risk via products:** under Article 6, an AI system is high-risk when it is a safety component of a product in Annex I that needs third-party conformity assessment.
- **AI Act timing:** the AI Act Explorer lists Annex I high-risk rules as applying from 2 August 2028.

> **Key idea:** In the EU, standards are voluntary but laws are not; standards are how you prove you meet the law.

> **Watch out:** This is a summary of official pages, not legal advice; dates have been amended, so recheck them before a real product.

## Key terms
- **CE marking**: The label showing a product meets EU requirements and may circulate in the single market.
- **Harmonised standard**: A voluntary standard whose use gives presumption of meeting legal requirements.
- **Safety component**: A part whose failure would endanger health and safety.
- **Conformity assessment**: The process proving a product meets the rules, sometimes by a third party.
- **Notified body**: An organisation designated to perform third-party conformity assessment.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Robot safety standards & risk assessment.
- **After:** Semantic safety & guardrails for LLM/VLA-controlled robots and Safe learning & safety filters, now read through the lens of the AI Act.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Pick one lab robot:** for example an arm running a learned policy at a public demo.
2. **Read the Commission page:** note which Machinery Directive or Regulation dates apply to your demo.
3. **Classify features:** for each AI feature, ask whether its failure would endanger health and safety (Article 6).
4. **Draft a checklist:** list risk assessment, instructions, declaration of conformity and CE marking items.

lessons.name: Safe learning & safety filters
lessons.summary: A safety filter sits between a learned policy and the motors and changes unsafe commands as little as possible, so the robot stays inside a safe set.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
A safety filter sits between a learned policy and the motors and changes unsafe commands as little as possible, so the robot stays inside a safe set.

![Diagram comparing model-driven, data-driven and combined approaches to a safe region](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-safety-filters.webp)
*Model-driven, data-driven and combined views of the safe region, from the safe-control-gym repository. Source: [safe-control-gym on GitHub](https://github.com/utiasDSL/safe-control-gym), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Learned policies surprise you:** a VLA can finish a task while knocking over unrelated objects, so task success does not prove safety.
- **Training-free fix:** a 2026 shield filtered a pretrained VLA's commands and cut simulated collisions from 65.62% to 27.27% without retraining.
- **Sim-only start:** safe-control-gym runs on PyBullet and costs nothing but a laptop.

## How it works
A safety filter is like **input validation middleware**: every request passes through, and only invalid ones are rewritten. The policy stays unchanged.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Sensors] --> B[Learned policy]
  B --> C[Proposed command]
  C --> D[Safety filter]
  A --> D
  D --> E[Safe command]
  E --> F[Motors]
```

- **Safe set:** define a function h(state) that is positive when safe, for example distance to an obstacle minus a margin.
- **Control barrier function (CBF):** a tool to enforce that the system never leaves that set, surveyed by Ames et al.
- **Barrier rule in words:** h may shrink, but slower as it nears zero; written dh/dt ≥ -α·h with α > 0.
- **Minimal change:** the filter solves a small optimization picking the allowed command closest to the policy's command.
- **Safe RL:** instead of filtering afterwards, constraints are added during learning; Brunke et al. review both families.

> **Key idea:** Keep the clever learned policy and the provable safety rule in separate boxes, so each can be checked on its own.

> **Watch out:** A filter only protects against constraints you modelled; an unmodelled hazard passes straight through.

## Key terms
- **Safety filter**: A runtime layer that minimally modifies unsafe actions from any controller.
- **Control barrier function**: A function whose sign marks safe states, used to keep a system inside them.
- **Safe set**: All states where the constraints hold.
- **Constraint**: A rule such as a position limit or minimum distance the system must respect.
- **Safe RL**: Reinforcement learning that encourages or enforces constraint satisfaction while learning.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Reinforcement learning for robots and basic feedback control.
- **After:** Speed & separation monitoring implementation, Semantic safety & guardrails for LLM/VLA-controlled robots and Safety of humanoids & dynamically stable mobile robots.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Write a 1D robot:** position x, velocity command u, wall at x = 1, in plain Python.
2. **Define h:** set h = 1 - x and a "policy" that always commands full speed toward the wall.
3. **Filter the command:** clip u to at most α·h, which satisfies the barrier rule for this simple model.
4. **Compare runs:** plot x with and without the filter for two values of α.
5. **Go further:** install safe-control-gym and read how it declares constraints on its cart-pole task.

lessons.name: Safety of humanoids & dynamically stable mobile robots
lessons.summary: A walking or self-balancing robot cannot just cut power in an emergency, because falling is itself a hazard, so its safe stop must be actively controlled.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
A walking or self-balancing robot cannot just cut power in an emergency, because falling is itself a hazard, so its safe stop must be actively controlled.

![Humanoid robot emergency-stop experiments with a digital twin and a safety-confidence plot](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-humanoids.webp)
*PRISM overview: a monitor predicts whether a fallback controller can still stop the humanoid safely. Source: [CMU Intelligent Control Lab](https://intelligent-control-lab.github.io/humanoid_stoppability/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Affordable humanoids:** Unitree lists the G1 from US $13.5K, so humanoids are reaching labs and demo floors.
- **Certification gap:** a 2026 paper argues industrial humanoids are limited less by skills than by immature functional-safety certification.
- **Demo planning:** any public humanoid demo needs a stop plan that does not end in an uncontrolled fall.

## How it works
Classic machine safety assumes **fail-passive**: remove power and the machine becomes safe. A biped is more like a server that must flush its state before shutdown; pulling the plug corrupts everything.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Stop requested] --> B{Monitor: safe-stoppable?}
  B -- yes --> C[Fallback controller]
  C --> D[Minimum-risk posture]
  B -- no --> E[Keep balancing policy]
  E --> B
```

- **Fail-passive gap:** removing power from a walking biped causes an uncontrolled fall, which violates the assumption behind ISO 13849-1 and EN 60204-1.
- **Stop Category 0:** contactor-based power removal is the certifiable reaction subsystem, exactly what a balancing humanoid cannot use.
- **Safe-stoppability:** PRISM learns a runtime monitor predicting whether a fixed fallback controller can still reach a minimum-risk condition from the current state.
- **Context-aware compliance:** SafeHumanoid uses a VLM with retrieval to schedule arm impedance and speed near people; latency reaches 1.4 s.

> **Key idea:** For a balancing robot, "safe state" is something the controller must actively reach, not something power removal gives you.

> **Watch out:** Never test emergency stops on a real humanoid without a gantry or harness; an unsupported fall can injure people nearby.

## Key terms
- **Dynamically stable robot**: A robot that stays upright only through active control, like a biped or a self-balancing wheeled base.
- **Fail-passive**: A design that becomes safe when power or control is lost.
- **Minimum-risk condition**: A terminal posture, such as crouched or seated, where the robot poses least danger.
- **Fallback controller**: A predefined controller that takes over to bring the robot to that condition.
- **Functional safety**: Safety that depends on control systems working correctly, rated with levels like PL or SIL.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Robot safety standards & risk assessment and RL locomotion with sim-to-real.
- **After:** Safe learning & safety filters applied to whole-body policies, and Speed & separation monitoring implementation for humanoid cells.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Watch a talk:** note what the Synapticon talk says about stopping a humanoid safely.
2. **Load a humanoid model:** open a free humanoid model in MuJoCo or another simulator.
3. **Cut torques mid-walk:** zero all motor commands during a gait and record how it falls.
4. **Script a fallback:** command a crouch posture instead and compare peak base speed with the uncontrolled fall.

lessons.name: Semantic safety & guardrails for LLM/VLA-controlled robots
lessons.summary: When an LLM or VLA controls a robot, safety also means judging meaning: refusing harmful instructions and checking plans against safety rules before the robot acts.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
When an LLM or VLA controls a robot, safety also means judging meaning: refusing harmful instructions and checking plans against safety rules before the robot acts.

![RoboGuard architecture: safety rules, a root-of-trust LLM, control synthesis and a mobile robot](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-guardrails.webp)
*RoboGuard grounds safety rules in a world model, then repairs the LLM planner's proposed plan. Source: [RoboGuard project page](https://robo-guard.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Real attacks work:** RoboPAIR jailbroke a GPT-3.5-integrated Unitree Go2 and a GPT-4o-planned Jackal, often with 100% attack success.
- **Guardrails help:** RoboGuard cut execution of unsafe plans from over 92% to below 3% without hurting safe plans.
- **Our stack:** any language-commanded SO-101 demo inherits these risks.

## How it works
It is the robotics version of **prompt injection defence plus a type checker**. The planner proposes; an independent checker verifies against rules it cannot be talked out of.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[User instruction] --> B[LLM planner]
  B --> C[Proposed plan]
  D[Safety rules] --> E[Guardrail checker]
  C --> E
  E -- safe --> F[Robot executes]
  E -- unsafe --> G[Repair or refuse]
```

- **Jailbreaking:** RoboPAIR adapts chatbot jailbreak attacks to elicit harmful physical actions, in white-, gray- and black-box settings.
- **Root-of-trust LLM:** RoboGuard's checker LLM is shielded from user prompts and turns rules into context-specific temporal logic constraints.
- **Control synthesis:** the plan is then resolved against those constraints, minimally violating user preferences.
- **Semantic safety benchmarks:** Google DeepMind's ASIMOV builds undesirable situations from real scenes and hospital injury reports to test robot "brains".
- **Robot constitutions:** ASIMOV also auto-generates written behaviour rules to steer models via Constitutional AI.
- **Modular layers:** a 2026 position paper argues for separate monitoring and intervention layers across the autonomy stack.

> **Key idea:** Never let the same model that a user can talk to be the only thing deciding whether an action is safe.

> **Watch out:** Text guardrails do not replace physical limits; keep speed and force limits active underneath any LLM.

## Key terms
- **Semantic safety**: Safety that depends on understanding context, such as not handing a hot pan to a child.
- **Jailbreak**: A prompt that makes a model bypass its safety training.
- **Guardrail**: An independent layer that checks or blocks model outputs before they act.
- **Temporal logic**: A formal language for rules over time, such as "never enter the hallway".
- **Red teaming**: Deliberately attacking your own system to find failures.

## Before / after
- **Before:** LLM/VLM task planning & code-as-policies and Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs).
- **After:** Robotics regulation & compliance in the EU and Safe learning & safety filters as the physical layer beneath.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Write a tool API:** expose fake robot actions like move_to(place) and pick(object) to an LLM.
2. **Write rules:** list three safety rules in plain text, for example "never move toward a person".
3. **Add a checker:** use a second, separately prompted LLM call that approves or rejects each planned step.
4. **Red-team the checker:** try role-play prompts from the RoboPAIR page and log which ones get through.

lessons.name: Shared control & shared autonomy
lessons.summary: In shared control, a human steers the robot with a joystick or teleoperation and the robot blends that input with its own autonomy to help finish the task.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
In shared control, a human steers the robot with a joystick or teleoperation and the robot blends that input with its own autonomy to help finish the task.

![Robot arm frames and diagrams showing the joystick input meaning changing with robot confidence](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-shared-control.webp)
*As the robot grows confident about the goal (b), the same joystick input shifts from choosing the goal to fine manipulation. Source: [Shared Autonomy with Learned Latent Actions](https://arxiv.org/html/2005.03210), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Assistive use:** shared autonomy helps people with motor impairments control robot arms for everyday tasks like eating.
- **Better training data:** BlenDAgger blends human and policy actions during corrections and gained 30+ points on two real tasks over HG-DAgger.
- **Sim-only start:** a joystick-plus-assistant demo needs no hardware.

## How it works
Think of **autocomplete in an editor**: you type, it guesses what you mean, and it fills in more as its guess gets confident. You can always keep typing to override.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Human joystick input] --> B[Goal inference]
  C[Scene: candidate goals] --> B
  B --> D[Robot assistive action]
  A --> E[Arbitration / blending]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Robot arm]
```

- **Goal inference:** the user's goal is often unknown in advance, so the robot infers it from their input.
- **Arbitration:** a blending rule mixes user and robot actions, giving the robot more weight as confidence rises.
- **Model-free option:** Reddy et al. learn assistance with deep RL, discarding low-value actions and picking the one closest to the user's input.
- **Latent actions:** a low-dimensional joystick can map to useful high-dimensional arm motions.
- **Legibility problem:** shortest-path assistance can hide which goal the robot inferred, so users keep steering or notice errors late.

> **Key idea:** The human stays in charge of intent, the robot takes over the precise, tiring parts, and control shifts with confidence.

> **Watch out:** Too much assistance toward a wrong guess feels like the robot fighting the user; always let input override it.

## Key terms
- **Shared autonomy**: Combining user input with semi-autonomous control toward a common goal.
- **Arbitration**: The rule deciding how much each side's command counts.
- **Goal inference**: Estimating which target the user wants from their inputs.
- **Teleoperation**: Directly driving a robot remotely, for example with a joystick.
- **Latent action**: A compact control signal decoded into full robot motion.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Basic teleoperation and Human motion & intention prediction.
- **After:** Learning from human feedback & corrections and Legible & expressive robot motion.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Build a 2D world:** draw a point "gripper" and three goal dots in Python.
2. **Read input:** move the point with arrow keys as the user command.
3. **Infer the goal:** score each goal by how well recent inputs point toward it.
4. **Blend commands:** mix user input with a step toward the top goal, weighted by its score.
5. **Compare effort:** count keypresses needed with and without assistance.

lessons.name: Social & human-aware navigation
lessons.summary: Social navigation means a mobile robot reaches its goal among people while respecting personal space, not cutting through groups, and moving predictably.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Social navigation means a mobile robot reaches its goal among people while respecting personal space, not cutting through groups, and moving predictably.

![HuNavSim architecture: simulator wrapper, ROS 2 services, HuNav manager with behavior trees and evaluator](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-social-navigation.webp)
*HuNavSim connects any robotics simulator through a wrapper and computes human agents plus social metrics. Source: [HuNavSim on GitHub](https://github.com/robotics-upo/hunav_sim), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Real deployments:** delivery, hospital and event robots move through crowds, not empty maps.
- **Hard to evaluate:** success depends on how people perceive the robot, not only on reaching the goal.
- **Free tooling:** HuNavSim and Arena run on ROS 2 in simulation, so starting costs €0.

## How it works
Normal path planning treats people as moving obstacles. Social navigation is closer to **UX design**: the "user" is every pedestrian, and comfort counts as much as speed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Sensors] --> B[People tracking]
  B --> C[Social cost map]
  D[Goal] --> E[Planner, e.g. Nav2]
  C --> E
  E --> F[Robot motion]
  F --> G[Social metrics]
```

- **Principles:** a 2023 guidelines paper lists safety, comfort, legibility, politeness, social competency, agent understanding, proactivity and context responsiveness.
- **Simulated humans:** HuNavSim moves people with a Social Force Model, including groups.
- **Human reactions:** agents can be regular, impassive, surprised, curious, scared or threatening toward the robot.
- **Benchmark loop:** a ROS 2 service returns updated human states each step; an evaluator computes social metrics.
- **Scenario generation:** Arena 4.0 uses LLMs and diffusion models to build human-centric worlds from text prompts or floorplans.

> **Key idea:** A socially good path is judged by the people around it, so you must measure comfort and predictability, not just arrival time.

## Key terms
- **Social Force Model**: A model where people are pushed by goals and repelled by obstacles and others.
- **Personal space**: The area around a person that others avoid entering.
- **Legibility**: How easily people can tell where the robot is going.
- **Cost map**: A grid giving each cell a cost the planner tries to minimize.
- **Benchmark**: A shared set of scenarios and metrics to compare methods fairly.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Basic mobile navigation with ROS 2 Nav2 and Human detection & body-pose tracking for HRI.
- **After:** Human motion & intention prediction for crowds and Legible & expressive robot motion.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Read the README:** go through HuNavSim's features and the list of human behaviors.
2. **Sketch a cost:** in Python, add a Gaussian cost around each person on a grid.
3. **Plan twice:** run A* with and without the social cost.
4. **Measure comfort:** compare minimum distance to people and path length for both paths.

lessons.name: Speed & separation monitoring implementation
lessons.summary: Speed and separation monitoring continuously measures the distance between robot and person and slows or stops the robot so it can always halt before contact.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence
Speed and separation monitoring continuously measures the distance between robot and person and slows or stops the robot so it can always halt before contact.

![Real UR10 cell with a person and motion capture next to its digital twin in simulation](/img/lessons/knowledge_hri_safety-separation.webp)
*A UR10 with three on-robot time-of-flight arrays, validated against a motion-capture digital twin. Source: [Kumar, Arora and Sahin, arXiv 1904.07379](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.07379), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us
- **Standard mode:** ISO/TS 15066 covers collaborative robot systems, and SSM is one of two risk-reduction approaches next to power and force limiting.
- **No cage needed:** the robot works at full speed when nobody is near, and slows only as someone approaches.
- **Cheap prototype:** a depth camera plus pose tracking can drive a demo on a desk arm.

## How it works
It works like **adaptive cruise control** for an arm: measure the gap, compute how fast you may go and still stop in time, repeat every cycle.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Sensors: ToF, RGB-D, lidar] --> B[Detect human]
  B --> C[Min distance robot-human]
  D[Robot link positions] --> C
  C --> E[Speed scaling rule]
  E --> F[Robot speed command]
  F --> D
```

- **Distance first:** compute the minimum distance between every robot link and the person, not just the gripper.
- **Relative velocity:** Kumar et al. modulate speed from both minimum distance and relative velocity.
- **Self-occlusion:** on-robot sensors also see the robot itself, so ray casting filters those readings out.
- **Keypoint pairs:** an RGB-D approach measures distance between all robot and human skeleton keypoints using OpenPose.
- **Validation:** compare your sensor distances against ground truth, such as motion capture or a 2D lidar.

> **Key idea:** The robot may only move as fast as it can still stop before reaching the nearest person.

> **Watch out:** Research prototypes like these are not certified safety functions; a hobby camera pipeline must not protect real people alone.

## Key terms
- **SSM**: Speed and separation monitoring, keeping a protective distance by scaling speed.
- **Protective separation distance**: The minimum gap required for the robot to stop in time.
- **Time-of-flight sensor**: A sensor that measures distance by timing reflected light.
- **Digital twin**: A simulated copy of the real cell used for testing.
- **Speed scaling**: Reducing commanded speed as a function of distance.

## Before / after
- **Before:** Collaborative operation modes (cobots) and Human detection & body-pose tracking for HRI.
- **After:** Collision detection & reaction (power and force limiting) and Safe learning & safety filters.

## Try it in an afternoon
1. **Track a person:** run MediaPipe Pose on a webcam and keep shoulder keypoints.
2. **Fake a robot:** pick a fixed 2D point on screen as the robot.
3. **Compute distance:** take the minimum pixel distance between keypoints and that point.
4. **Scale speed:** map distance to 0–100% speed with stop and full-speed thresholds, and display it.
